text: A virtual machine includes a complete guest operating system, its own kernel and drivers, running on top of the hypervisor's virtual hardware. A container skips all of that — it shares the host's existing kernel and only packages the application along with its own libraries. That one difference, a full duplicate OS per VM versus one shared kernel for every container, is the entire reason these two technologies behave so differently.

If every container shares the host's kernel, what stops one from seeing another's files or processes? Two real Linux kernel features. Namespaces give each container its own isolated view of process IDs, network interfaces, and mount points, so one container literally can't see another's processes. Cgroups limit how much CPU, memory, and I-O each container is allowed to consume, so one can't starve the others on the same host.

That's why containers start so much faster. Starting a VM means booting an entire operating system from scratch — loading a kernel, starting services — which realistically takes thirty seconds to a couple of minutes. Starting a container means launching a single process inside namespaces that already exist on an already-running kernel, which is why containers routinely start in well under a second.

The same gap shows up in resource usage: ten VMs means ten full operating system copies sitting in memory, while ten containers sharing one image typically only duplicate the application layer itself — far lighter on the same hardware.

So when do you actually pick one? Choose a VM when you need a different OS than the host, or the strongest possible isolation between tenants. Choose a container when fast startup and high density matter more, like microservices or CI/CD pipelines. In practice, most production environments run both — containers for the app layer, on top of VMs for the underlying infrastructure.

That closes the container-versus-VM comparison. Lesson 22 ties everything in this chapter together by showing exactly how public cloud providers build their entire business on top of massive hypervisor fleets.
